### Part A — Creating, Sorting, and Indexing Data
```{r}
# 1a. Create named vector of student scores
scores <- c("Ana" = 78, "Ben" = 92, "Cid" = 85, "Dex" = 92, "Eli" = 67, "Fay" = 88, "Gio" = 74)
scores

# 1b. Sort scores in ascending and descending order
sort(scores)
sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)

# 1c. Print sorted scores to verify names stayed attached
print(sort(scores))

# 1d. Create additional vectors: subjects and incomplete
subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "PE")
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)

# 1e. Sort subjects alphabetically
sort(subjects)

# 1f. Sort incomplete with na.last = TRUE so NAs appear at the end
sort(incomplete, na.last = TRUE)
```
Question #2

Names staying attached during sort and why it matters:

Yes, names stayed attached because the values were defined as a named vector. If names detached during sorting, scores would be assigned to the wrong students, misidentifying top and bottom performers.

Question #3

Danger of sort() silently omitting NA values:

By default, sort() drops NA values without warning. If missing scores were lower than recorded ones, reporting the default minimum would give a false lowest score.

### Part B — Comparing sort() vs order()
```{r}
# Display raw order indices vs sorted values
order(scores)
sort(scores)

# Indexing scores with order(scores)
scores[order(scores)]
```
Question #4

Difference between order(scores) and sort(scores):

sort(scores) returns the actual data values rearranged in order. order(scores) returns the original index positions needed to achieve sorted order. Indexing scores[order(scores)] yields the exact same output as sort(scores) because it retrieves elements by those ordered positions.

### Part C — Sorting Data Frames with order()
```{r}
# 5a. Create the students data frame
students <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio"),
  score = c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74),
  section = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")
)
students

# 5b. Reorder students data frame by score (ascending)
students[order(students$score), ]

# 5c. Reorder students data frame by score (descending)
students[order(-students$score), ]
```

Question #6

What order(scores) returns and why it requires indexing:

order(scores) returns raw index numbers representing row positions. On its own, it is just a list of position numbers; it becomes useful only when passed into index brackets [ ] to reorder vectors or entire data frame rows.

Question #7

Why sort() cannot reorder a data frame while order() can:

sort() extracts and rearranges a single vector, losing row associations. order() returns positional indices, allowing df[order(...), ] to move entire rows together so all columns stay aligned.

### Part D — Ranking Data and Handling Ties
```{r}
# 8a. Compute rank of scores and display side-by-side
rank(scores)
cbind(scores, rank = rank(scores))

# Display ranks specifically for Ben and Dex
rank(scores)[c("Ben", "Dex")]
```

Question #8

Tied ranks for Ben and Dex:

Ben and Dex both receive a rank of 6.5. They share the 6th and 7th highest score positions (92). R's default rank() computes the average of tied positions (6 + 7) / 2 = 6.5 to treat tied observations fairly.

### Part E — Sales Ranking Challenge
```{r}
# 9a. Create sales data frame and add rank column (top seller = rank 1)
sales <- data.frame(
  employee = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"),
  units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130)
)

sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold)
sales

# 9b. Reorder sales data frame from HIGHEST to LOWEST units_sold
sales[order(-sales$units_sold), ]
```

Question #9

Why order() alone cannot replace rank() for tied standings:

order() breaks ties arbitrarily to output a strict sequence of unique row positions. It lacks tie-handling logic, whereas rank() identifies identical values and assigns them equal numerical standings.
